item.content:encoded:
This conversation plays out hundreds of times a day, but (thankfully) only a handful of those involve me:

  • Person: “I have [problem].”
  • Cryptography nerd: “Oh, you probably want to use [sensible recommendation].”
  • Person: “Ah, well, can I really trust that? The NSA probably backdoored it 30 years ago. Dual_EC, amirite?!”
  • Cryptography nerd: …
  • Koblitz and Menezes, unheard: “You fucking wot m8?“

Conspiracy theories about the NSA and/or NIST are a dime a dozen these days. And, ever since the Snowden disclosures in 2013, I am politically primed to directionally agree with distrusting the US government wholesale.

But most of the technical arguments baked into folks’ conspiracy theories make no goddamn sense.

This distrust is not exclusive to only the US government.

The goal of this blog post is not to convince you that you should trust any government; just that they are not magical or omniscient.

To that end, I’m going to explore some of the history of NSA, NIST, and cryptography standardization. Then, to explore some of the conspiracy theories that were being floated about such activity, and what we’ve learned in the years since (especially in the past month). Finally, I’m going to examine some of the current conspiracy theories floating around message boards and social media today, and explain why they’re almost certainly wrong.

Buckle up, this is going to be a tedious one.

Why should we listen to you?

If you find yourself asking a question like this, the correct answer is simply, “You shouldn’t.”

After all, I have never held (let alone even applied for) a security clearance, and have no access to any non-public information. I’m also not a current or former government employee, and have no aspirations to ever become one. I have access to all the same facts anyone else does.

In balance, I have no horse in the race of who trusts whom. I’m just tired of hearing the same poorly reasoned arguments all the damn time, and would like to stop having to repeat myself when I encounter one.

Historical NSA Shenanigans

The sources for this, by the way, are the declassified United States Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and United States Cryptologic History.

DES

The Data Encryption Standard (DES) was published in the Federal Register in 1975 and then standardized in 1977.

We consider it weak these days, but DES was a real game-changer for its time: It offered a standard block cipher to use for sensitive (but not classified) commercial applications. Prior to DES, the history of cryptography was largely about military uses (except a few quirky mathematicians here and there), going back before Caesar’s cipher.

From declassified documents, we now know the full story, but from the time that DES was first standardized, up until recent years, there have been a concerns about NSA’s involvement.

We sent the S-boxes off to Washington. They came back and were all different.

Alan Konheim, quoted in Applied Cryptography, p. 280

To say that academics did not trust DES would be putting it mildly: Martin Hellman (who, with Whitfield Diffie and Ralph Merkle, invented public-key cryptography) sent a letter in 1975 to the National Bureau of Standards that stated:

Whit Diffie and I have become concerned that the proposed data encryption standard, while probably secure against commercial assault, may be extremely vulnerable to attack by an intelligence organization.

Martin Hellman, re-published in this paper in 1990.

At the heart of the concern about DES was something called an S-box, which simply maps an input to an output, but whose purpose is to provide a non-linear transformation to obscure the relationship between the ciphertext and the key.

The S-box used by DES was chosen by NSA. This led a lot of people to suspect there was a backdoor in the selection of the S-boxes for DES. It turned out to be the opposite, of course: The NSA had discovered differential cryptanalysis in secret, and had selected S-boxes that were resistant to this technique, but did not want to reveal it publicly (lest they lose their advantage over rival nations).

There’s a lot more details to this story than I want to bore anyone with, so I recommend reading up on the history of cryptography and cryptanalysis if you’re interested in such things.

In balance, at the advice of NSA, the final DES design did only offer 56 bits of security (down from an original key size of 128 bits). This short key ultimately allowed the EFF to crack DES in 1998 with a hardware cost of about $250,000.

What does this actually tell us?

When IBM was designing DES, with feedback from NSA, the stated purpose was to use for commercial cryptographic applications in the United States.

Fact: NSA used secret cryptanalytic capabilities to ensure the resulting block cipher that became DES was protected from the attack they knew about without revealing said technique.

Fact: NSA recommended reducing the key length from 128 bits to 64 bits (with 8 of the key bits serving as parity bits, thus making it only have 56-bit security).

This both strengthened and weakened DES in different ways. A 56-bit key can be broken by a distributed computing effort in under 24 hours, as of 2012.

This is confusing until you remember NSA has two opposing missions, with (unfortunately) military jargon names.

  • COMSEC (Communications Security) — basically blue-teamers
  • SIGINT (Signals Intelligence) — basically red-teamers

The COMSEC folks have a mission to secure the US government and protect US interests (read: private sector).

The SIGINT folks have a mission to spy on other nations on behalf of the US.

In theory, the SIGINT folks aren’t supposed to spy on Americans at all. In practice, their Five Eyes partners gives them a stupid loophole: An allied nation can simply do the spying for them, so long as federal prosecutors are willing to engage in a little bit of parallel construction.

Take note of the DEA section of the previously linked Wikipedia page.

You cannot trust the government, but if you know the mission each department operates under, you can understand their incentive structures. Knowing their incentive structures lets you reason about their actual activities–or, failing that, create conspiracy theories with a cohesive narrative.

The COMSEC mission can be related to the S-box strengthening; the SIGINT mission, to the weaker key length.

Clipper Chip

Okay, so the DES thing was a messy affair. Let’s look at an example of the NSA clearly being on the wrong side of privacy.

The Clipper Chip, which was designed and promoted by the NSA in 1993 to secure voice messages, with a backdoor.

Clipper Chip was an early example of a NOBUS (Nobody But Us can exploit it) backdoor. Unlike DES’s 56-bit key, the cipher used (Skipjack) was promoted up to a whopping 80-bits.

But before you celebrate, be aware that there was a “key escrow” feature that allowed law enforcement to decrypt plaintext, and a 16-bit hash in the “Law Enforcement Access Field” (LEAF) that turned out to be a pretty stupid vulnerability, as Matt Blaze discovered in 1994. If you want a technical breakdown, Professor Matt Green’s blog post covers this (and other backdoors).

Not only was the Clipper Chip a terrible idea to begin with, it was also technically flawed (to the point of embarrassment). This was the first of many issues in what became known as the Crypto Wars.

What does this actually tell us?

When the NSA colluded with law enforcement to spy on Americans’ private conversations, their attempt was met with public backlash from independent technologists (Matt Blaze, the Electronic Frontier Foundation, etc.).

The cryptography community outside the military-industrial complex today is largely primed to call out Clipper Chip style bullshit whenever it happens. (See also: the EU’s ChatControl.)

Dual_EC_DRBG

In 2006, NIST published SP 800-90, which recommended deterministic random bit generators (DRBGs):

  • Hash_DRBG — generating random bits from cryptographic hash functions computed over input entropy sources
  • HMAC_DRBG — generating random bits from HMAC (which is kind of like if a hash function had a secret key)
  • CTR_DRBG — turning a block cipher into a random bit stream by using Counter Mode

The three I listed above are… well, they’re fine. Pretty much everyone uses hash functions or block ciphers to squeeze random bits out of smaller amounts of entropy.

But the fourth entry in the NIST standard was an odd duck. Dual_EC_DRBG was several times slower than the other recommendations and was immediately flagged as having a backdoor (which other cryptographers agreed with).

I don’t understand why the NSA was so insistent about including Dual_EC_DRBG in the standard. It makes no sense as a trap door: It’s public, and rather obvious. It makes no sense from an engineering perspective: It’s too slow for anyone to willingly use it. And it makes no sense from a backwards-compatibility perspective: Swapping one random-number generator for another is easy.

My recommendation, if you’re in need of a random-number generator, is not to use Dual_EC_DRBG under any circumstances. If you have to use something in SP 800-90, use CTR_DRBG or Hash_DRBG.

In the meantime, both NIST and the NSA have some explaining to do.

Bruce Schneier, Wired, 2007

Of course, because of Edward Snowden, we know today that cryptographers were completely correct about Dual_EC_DRBG being a backdoor by the NSA.

Ever since that revelation, no discussion about NOBUS (Nobody But Us) backdoors would be complete without at least mentioning Dual_EC_DRBG.

What almost nobody foresaw, however, was that a rival nation state would replace the public key baked into Dual_EC’s design with their own while backdooring Juniper Networks.

Kind of a stupid fucking approach to NOBUS, ain’t it?

What does this actually tell us?

When the incentives of the NSA aligned with malicious government conspiracies against the American people (sorry to keep specifying this, by the way, but they’re pretty much always malicious to folks outside the USA) and standardization processes, it didn’t fly under the radar and basically every cryptographer said “Hell no” to using it.

Whether NSA is capable of being sneakier while corrupting NIST documents remains to be seen.

The Snowden Disclosures

There’s far too much to talk about here, and of varying usefulness. Consult the Snowden Archives if you want to read more. There were a lot of codenames. There was a lot of jargon.

It spawned a lot of memes.

Some of the codenames (e.g., FOXACID) are the sort of thing that cause eyebrows to raise among computer nerds that are familiar with furries and vore.

Here’s a lightning round of some of what we learned from Snowden:

  1. Bulk collection of Americans’ phone metadata, despite James Clapper committing perjury to the contrary
  2. PRISM: mass passive surveillance of the Internet, which is largely why TLS became ubiquitous in the years since.
  3. Tempora: copied data from undersea cables for NSA to analyze
  4. BULLRUN / EDGEHILL — see also: Dual_EC_DRBG, but also RSA Security
  5. XKeyscore: basically a private version of Palantir’s product today

There’s so much more we could talk about, but what’s notably absent from Snowden’s leaks is any secret cryptanalytic attacks against standardized cryptography.

Notably, they couldn’t break Tor in any way that wasn’t already known to the Tor developers at the time.

Hell, there were myriad conspiracy theories in late 2013 about the Silk Road marketplace being taken down by a NSA attack on Tor. The slide decks Snowden leaked suggest otherwise.

What does this actually tells us?

A lot. Far too much, in fact, for me to dissect it all in this blog post!

But the pertinent detail is this: The absence of cryptanalytic capabilities in Snowden’s leaks can be interpreted one of several ways.

  1. The private sector has largely caught up with NSA
  2. NSA’s compartmentalization was somehow successful at preventing Snowden from discovering these mathematical techniques, but not all the other damning evidence
  3. The NSA didn’t bother trying to beat the cryptography because it was, as is often the case today, so much easier to simply bypass it entirely

Personally, I think any of these interpretations is valid. I’d put my money on number 3, of course. After all, that’s what PRISM largely did.

People Can’t Be Normal About This

I omitted several controversies from the previous section, because it was getting too long and I feel I justified my point already. However, I’m sure some people will cry foul at omissions as an attempt at deception, so I need to also mention one that was recently solved.

The NIST P-Curve Seeds

The what now?

Elliptic curve cryptography is a whole topic I’ve talked about on this blog before, at length, but I’m going to simplify for the sake of being somewhat comprehensible to people who don’t make Frobenius trace jokes on IRC.

NIST published FIPS 186-2 in 2000 (and later updated it in 2001), which provided several elliptic curve groups (P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, P-521).

Each elliptic curve group was parametrized by a seed, s, which was never explained by NSA. The output of the SHA-1 hash of s was used to calculate the parameters for each elliptic curve group.

Jerry Solinas, who was the mathematician and cryptographer that published the P-curves, couldn’t remember how the seeds were chosen.

In the wake of Dual_EC_DRBG and BULLRUN, any unexplained value being the basis of several NIST standardized elliptic curve groups caused many people to be itchy.

For a while, Daniel J. Bernstein’s Curve25519 algorithms and software gained popularity in the applied cryptography spaces. This was probably a good thing, overall, but there were some sharp edges (that later work has since improved upon).

Speaking from experience, many of these decisions post-Snowden were the result of paranoia about the NSA possibly adding a NOBUS backdoor to the NIST P-Curves too, rather than merely for the technical merits of Curve25519.

However, Koblitz and Menezes already tackled that in a paper titled, “A Riddle Wrapped In An Enigma.” To summarize their mathematical arguments: If NSA was aware of a secret weakness that only occurs in some number of elliptic curve groups, and wanted to make a NOBUS backdoor that their adversaries couldn’t figure out, it would need to be a structural weakness that only occurs extremely rarely.

So rarely, in fact, that not only would the computational resources available to Jerry Solinas in the late 1990s would not have been sufficient, but you still couldn’t do it today.

This scenario is highly implausible for several reasons. First, the class of weak curves must be extremely large in order to obtain a weak curve with the seeded-hash method. For concreteness, suppose that p is a fixed 256-bit prime. There are roughly isomorphism classes of elliptic curves defined over . Let be the proportion of elliptic curves over that are believed (by everyone except hypothetically the NSA in 1997) to be safe. This class of curves includes essentially all elliptic curves of prime order (with the exception of prime-field anomalous curves and those that succumb to the Weil/Tate pairing attack). Since the proportion of 256-bit numbers that are prime is approximately , the proportion of curves that are strong is at least . Now suppose that the proportion of these curves that the NSA knew how to break were . In this hypothetical scenario the NSA could select such a weak curve by trying about seeds. The number of NSA-weak curves would then be approximately . This would mean that this huge class of weak curves was known to the NSA in 1997 but is still undiscovered by outside researchers in 2015. It is highly unlikely that such a large family of weak elliptic curves would have escaped detection by the cryptographic research community from 1997 to the present.

Koblitz and Menezes, 2015 (emphasis mine)

This quote highlights my broader point in this whole blog post: The NSA isn’t magical. (Nor is AI. Nor are quantum computers.) The NSA’s capabilities and budgets are finite. Their incentives are defined by their mission.

In 2023, Filippo Valsorda and several others (including myself) pledged a bounty (with extra if the award is donated to charity) to anyone that could solve the mystery of the NIST P-curve seeds.

Earlier this month, Anthropic successfully claimed that bounty, and elected to donate the bounty to the ISRG (the non-profit that operates the Let’s Encrypt certificate authority).

There’s a poetic irony here: My pledged donation is going towards the organization that led the way to making TLS ubiquitous online since 2015 in the wake of the NSA’s global mass surveillance… because one of the NSA mysteries was finally solved.

This is a nice segue into the final topic I want to discuss today.

Post-Quantum Cryptography

I’ve already covered most of what I want to say here in a previous post titled, Hybrid Constructions: The Post-Quantum Safety Blanket.

I was tagged in a Fediverse post yesterday that punctuated the sort of discourse cryptographers have already seen in the IETF mailing list threads and on technical forums in the past few months:

NIST works for US fash regime that’s trying to help their AI scammer buddies pivot to quantum scams.

That’s the generous interpretation.

The worse one is that NSA has known flaws/backdoors in the post quantum systems and wants to shut down the actually-secure ones.

@dalias@hachyderm.io – (To be clear, I chose this comment as an example because it’s more coherent than the others I’ve seen in 2026. Do NOT be a jerk to anyone.)

This was a reply to a quote-post of another thread that described NIST publishing its final plan for IR 8547: the transition to post-quantum cryptography.

The NSA announced, in 2015, its plans to migrate to “quantum resistant algorithms”.

For the decade or so since, the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography standardization effort has largely revolved around the NIST pqc-forum. You can read the archived email threads, publicly, going back to the forum’s inception. Most of the emails are dry, boring, technical, and/or procedural.

But in the beginning? It was a bloodbath of cryptanalytic attacks against proposed KEMs and signature algorithms.

The NIST recommendations and standards for post-quantum cryptography were a transparent effort involving virtually anyone in the cryptography and security communities that wanted to participate spanning from 2015 until now, and it is still ongoing.

The selected algorithms (i.e., ML-KEM, formerly known as CRYSTALS-Kyber) were designed by international teams. The principal submitter of ML-KEM, Peter Schwabe, even worked with Daniel J. Bernstein on NaCl in the 2010s (and was one of Bernstein’s Ph.D Students).

Bernstein, for those not following along, was a large source of irritation on the TLS Working Group mailing list earlier this year for his weird anti-ML-KEM and anti-ML-DSA tirades and concern-trolling.

At one point, he tried to summon Twitter mobs to join the mailing list and pack the vote… except, that’s not how Rough Consensus works at IETF at all!

Today, many “NIST backdoored post-quantum” conspiracy theories point to Bernstein to support their points.

It’s all very stupid and disappointing.

Furthermore, there isn’t enough structure in ML-KEM, in particular, to squeeze in a public key to make any plausible weakness truly NOBUS.

How plausible is an NSA backdoor here, really?

I’m no Neil Koblitz or Alfred Menezes, so forgive me if my rebuttal doesn’t contain the mathematical rigor of those two.

Here are some facts to consider.

  1. The federal government (through CNSA 2.0) is being told to adopt ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87. Hybrid constructions are not blessed for protecting federal government systems.
  2. As we saw with the DES S-boxes, the NSA is known to sometimes make decisions that improve security (though may conceal an attack on competing designs).
  3. NSA has a dual mission: COMSEC and SIGINT, as discussed above.
  4. NSA has tried to subvert standards before (DUAL_EC_DRBG).

Is it plausible that the NSA would be so confident in the NOBUS status of a secret flaw or backdoor in ML-KEM (which they did not design) that they’d move the entire fucking federal government’s systems for TOP SECRET classified information to adopt it as fast as possible?

I don’t know, man. That sounds kind of fucking stupid to me.

In my opinion, a more compelling conspiracy theory is that NSA already secretly built a quantum computer in their Utah data center, and it’s already being used to spy on everyone today.

It’s a better fit than “ML-KEM is a NSA backdoor, the European cryptographers that designed it are all stupid, and the NSA is eager to move the US government onto a flawed or broken cryptosystem because SIGINT is all they care about, even at the expense of COMSEC, and they also can’t just look for the plaintext (which already works 99% of the time) they gotta be able to crack the encryption” which is the essence of the conspiracy theories that keep hitting my inbox today.

Conspiracy theories aren’t harmless. They create room for grifters and hucksters to deceive well-intentioned non-experts.

In Closing

If you convinced yourself of a wrong conspiracy theory, that doesn’t mean you are dumb or unlovable.

NSA is certainly up to something. It’s their entire fucking job to be up to something. But it’d very unlikely to be a post-quantum backdoor no matter how much energy is expended on discussion boards and social media trying to convince people of that narrative.

Since neither you nor I have any information on what they’re actually up to, it’s tempting to look at the absence of evidence and fill-in-the-blanks and pattern-match based on what we already know today. That’s not stupidity.

Unfortunately, most of the proponents of these conspiracy theories will cherry-pick the most damning examples (i.e., Dual_EC_DRBG, through the lens of Snowden) while ignoring the messier and more nuanced aspects of the NSA’s [mis]conduct with the larger cryptography community.

So, please: Stay curious and humble. Better and more likely conspiracy theories exist, and may even be true, but you’ll never reach them if you short-circuit your analysis on stale low-hanging fruit and stop wondering.

item.content:encoded:
The problems with the furry fandom today are not as simple as,
“Furries need to touch grass!”

Unfortunately, whatever you’re seeing that makes you want to say such a thing is probably a structural problem with multiple compounding factors.

I will elaborate.

But first, for anyone who feels lost, I need to explain where we are and how we got here.

One of the downsides of furries continuing to use Twitter in 2026 is that they’re being boiling-frogged into the worst versions of themselves. If this never broke containment, it would merely be a digital version of Gu. Alas, it spills over onto every platform.

I’ve previously opined that, as furries leave Twitter in search of other platforms, BlueSky deserves to win the popularity contest (partly because I didn’t expect Mastodon to cope with a sudden deluge of users).

Unfortunately, every platform slowly became a different kind of Hitler, so there is no morally superior social media selection to be made.

Fortunately, I’m not here to preach about morals or take a stance of superiority. Instead, I want to highlight a pattern that many of us have recognized, draw a clean line between observation and impact, and then talk about some ideas for what we can do about this mess.

What Structural Means

EDIT: This section was added on 2026-10-04 after several people complained erroneously about the word “structural”.

When I say the furry fandom’s problems are “structural,” I mean they emerge from how the systems underpinning the furry fandom are setup.

Some of these systems have emergent properties; others are explicit and intentional.

Recommended reading on the subject:

  • The distinction between personal troubles and public issues
  • What “social structure” means in sociology
  • A Psychology Today explainer on the above

This isn’t referring to physical structures.

Root Causes

1. Society’s Third Places Are Virtually Nonexistent

The concept of a Third Place comes from sociology. That is, a place other than work and home that people can just vibe in.

We don’t have third places in America, these days.

This is not uniquely an American problem, but I can only speak to it from an American perspective. A recent write-up on Singapore’s new government-run dating service leads me to believe they have a similar issue, for example. Other countries might be less affected by this.

Every time I travel to Europe for a work-related event, I’m always surprised by how long everyone lingers at cafes chatting with each other, and even moreso, how tolerant the employees are of it.

The erasure of third places probably didn’t start with the removal of teenagers from shopping malls (using “loitering” laws to punish them for not spending [enough] money), but that was the evidence that first clued me into the phenomenon nearly twenty years ago.

When evangelical Christians try to tie social ills to lower church membership, they’re not actually wrong: The church was, historically, a “third place” to a lot of people. But the problem is much broader than just religious centers, and thus the solution shouldn’t be to prioritize any particular faith system.

This affects furries for one simple reason: We are part of society.

2. The Cameras Are Always On

In my generation and older, we developed social skills through what social scientists loosely call “experimentation”.

It’s normal for kids to go through “phases” where they try out new hobbies and interests. But it also used to be normal for kids to try new conversational habits, jokes, and so on with their peer groups. If the jokes didn’t land, they’d feel embarrassed for a few minutes but adapt and everyone would move on.

We don’t live in that world anymore. Someone making a crass joke has to calculate the risk of becoming the Main Character of Social Media for the day, which can lead to doxing, stalking, facing life-altering consequences, and even having their home swatted.

And it’s not necessarily the case that anyone’s friends are going to immediately try to cancel them into oblivion for the minor social offense of suggesting that a gay friend who likes dad jokes should adopt the drag name Ra-pun-zel (because they’re about to “let down their heir”). But you can never really predict what will be the Unforgivable Sin for the Online Mob today, so it’s better to just keep quiet.

And then they enter adulthood and discover that people who were not socially stunted by social media platforms don’t carry the same internalized shame they do, and thus the discouse propagates.

3. The Furry Fandom’s Growth

I wrote Furries Are Losing the Battle Against Scale in 2024, to highlight the impact of a 20-30% Year-over-Year exponential growth on the furry community as a whole.

It’s difficult to understate how much this affects everything going on right now. While convention attendance doubles roughly every three to five years (depending on the venue), con staff and volunteering grow linearly (if at all). This is not sustainable.

This has another consequence I didn’t call out in 2024: Your specialness in the furry fandom is inversely proportional to how many furries there are. When you combine this with root cause 2 (the cameras are always on), you get an exacerbation of influencer-brain.

The tactics that would make you stand out among 100,000 furries, and the tactics you need to get the same proportion of 1,000,000 furies talking about you, are very different.

You don’t have to be a self-proclaimed rockstar to fall into the same trappings of ego.

4. COVID-19 Lockdown

I cannot explain it better than TikTok user @msaleshadiva:

I’ve received a bit of pushback about this video’s inclusion on this blog post.

You don’t have to agree with 100% of what she says to see her points and how they can be applied to furry.

And, to be blunt, I’m not going to recontextualize or speak over women of color.

A similar dynamic plays out in this webcomic_name comic, if you don’t like videos:

A similar concept in computing spaces is the notion of the Eternal September: What used to be an influx of new users with poor netiquette every September when school starts became an endless deluge once the Internet became a household commodity rather than an academic curiosity.

When a subculture or counterculture becomes populous enough that it threatens to subsume pop culture, a lot of social friction occurs. This leads to cranks whining about furry pilots on the Senate floor as much as it leads to Twitter mobs trying to dox a new fursuiter.

5. Platforms, Algorithms, and Incentives

One of the more frustrating aspects of existing in 2026 is algo-speak.

It starts with the use of stupid euphemisms to talk about a subject without the censors (read: advertisers) realizing you’re talking about those subjects, so that you can practice free speech on a centralized, corporate controlled platform without losing ad revenue (which is often the creator’s entire incentive for participating).

But then it leaks out into the audience and shapes how people speak about things. For example, they’ll start saying things like “unalive” instead of directly talk about suicide. This doesn’t help anyone. In fact, it makes it harder for people sensitive to these topics to filter the posts out before they see them, especially if they have involuntary Pavlovian anxiety responses to such material (a.k.a. “triggers”). Instead of simple, honest, and direct communication with appropriate content warning keywords so the “Muted Words” feature works properly, people will go as far as to type their algo-speak, filter-evading euphemistic bullshit into images… and then not include alt-text, which fucks over the people with visual impairments to boot.

As annoying as that is (and, make no mistake, this trend does piss me off), it’s not entirely their fault. When your media diet consists entirely of people who will say “PDF file” instead of “pedophile” (or “paedophile” if they’re British), it takes a lot of unnecessary discipline to not mimic their tendencies.

Platforms have incentives. Platforms that use Recommendation Systems for content discovery (i.e., most of them) lead to maladaptive behaviors. Outrage, scandal, and spectacle tend to dominate people’s attention.

The owner class doesn’t care about the harms caused by their systems. They only care about their quarterly earnings report, because maximizing shareholder value is their north star for any decision they make.

What Can We Do?

The most important step into solving a problem is correctly identifying that you even have a problem to solve.

Sometimes, despite what frenzy has been whipped up online, there isn’t a problem to begin with. Let’s talk through some examples:

  • Someone had a bad take?
    Don’t engage with them. Unfollow, mute for 30 days (if your platform allows it) or however long it takes for things to cool down, don’t approach them at cons. Either they’ll learn, or they’ll double down. It’s not your problem either way, is it?

    You probably don’t need to go further than that. We all have the same 24 hours every day, why waste them on someone you dislike?
  • Someone had a messy break-up?
    Were they breaking up with you?
    Was anyone raped, assaulted, or worse?

    No??? Then there is no action necessary!
  • Someone is being a Christian Nationalist / white supremacist / [insert other hate group here]?
    Remove them immediately. They are a problem, no matter how nice or polite they seem. Remember the parable of Nazi bars.

    But otherwise, this problem is trivially solvable and doesn’t need a lot of deliberation, no?

When you do actually have a problem worth solving on your hands, look at the behavior you want to discourage and try to figure out the root cause. It might be one of the five I listed above, or it might be something else. My list is certainly not exhaustive!

But it’s pretty easy to see how:

  1. The lack of third places;
  2. The lack of judgment-free social experimentation in folks’ upbringing that won’t forever haunt them on social media;
  3. The explosive exponential growth of the furry fandom (which is itself a messy problem to contend with);
  4. The knock-on effects of COVID-19 lockdown which led a lot of “normal” and popular youths to get involved in niche fandom hobbies (including, but not limited to, furry); and
  5. The incentives of social media platforms

…can lead to a conflux of downstream problems including many of the annoyances we deal with today.

Depending on the problem you have in mind, a different set of causes might be behind it.

Fortunately, each of these problems is solvable, and you don’t have to be a Person Of Influence to enact most of them.

Unfortunately, none of the solutions are “easy.”

Low-Stakes Third Places For Furries

I mentioned this in my Scaling Issues blog post, but we need a lot more smaller, lower-stakes hang-outs for people in our community to hang out.

Conventions are great. I’m not telling anyone to stop going to conventions.

I’m saying that you should aspire to do more meetups, movie nights, bowling alley ventures, arcade escapades, and so on with your local furry groups. Maybe rent a pavilion at your community park, or pool money and rent an AirBNB for a weekend. Throw a barbecue. Be cringe and free.

Who knows? You might even become friends with more of them.

Whatever works for your local scene, I recommend not putting most of it on social media. The more poorly socialized a critter is, the less they’ll appreciate being bullied by strangers.

Small Community-Focused Efforts

If you’re going to conventions, consider volunteering for a few hours (even if it’s only on a day when you had nothing else planned anyway).

The scale issues I’ve been talking about for years are going to get worse, but everyone who steps up to relieve pressure from the convention organizers helps keep the fandom together while they figure it out.

If you’re familiar with the history of fandom discourse, take the time to explain the debates we’ve already had and the rough consensus we’ve settled on to newcomers. You were probably upset or curious about this at one point in your life too. Better to explain it once than watch people stumble over the same roadblocks and end up bitter over it.

If you’re not familiar with the history, please listen to your queer elders. We aren’t trying to police you or your fun. (We just ask that you don’t try to police us.)

The more people are willing to listen to each other, the less likely they are to shout.

Everyone being community-minded, even if only a little, will help make the fandom a more tolerable place for everyone worth tolerating.

Understand The Monster That Social Media Truly Is

The “go touch grass” sentiment (which I’ve also admittedly engaged in a few times over the years) is rooted in the idea that the other person is terminally Online and needs to quit cold turkey by going Offline for a while. Since grass is Offline, the act of touching it implies being offline. (People with grass allergies, sorry for any confusion.)

But you don’t need to do anything drastic or extreme.

Social media, for all its ills, can connect you to other people with shared interests and compatible personalities.

But under no circumstance should you EVER let the platforms control you or who you’re friends with. Recommendation systems are not the only algorithm at play in social media. Sometimes your friends will be shadow-banned or otherwise penalized and you’ll see less of them. One day you or them might abruptly get banned for “inauthentic behavior” (n.b., this happened to my After Dark Twitter account years after I stopped posting on it). These decisions will be made for irrational and arbitrary reasons.

Also: Not everything needs to be public, and you do not owe anyone a “face reveal”.

Focus On Real Problems

When I rallied furries to raise funds to save the Ridgeland Library from their homophobic mayor in 2022, that succeeded because it wasn’t just a furry problem, or even just a LGBTQ+ problem. Free speech and libraries are intertwined in America.

In a similar vein, while “who’s that new fursuiter?” is squarely answered with “who cares it’s none of my business”, there are real problems in the furry community. We have personality cults like Furry Valley running amok. We have sexual offenders like Jacob Kovar being protected by Colorado furry groups.

Closing Thoughts

We can, as a community, do better. We just have to understand what is causing a lot of the problems we see day-to-day and take steps to fix them.

I recognize that a lot of the solutions I’ve offered here are mid, at best. Unfortunately, just because I can point to the specific problems, doesn’t mean I know the best solutions to any of them.

This blog post isn’t a call to action for everyone to listen to me and follow my directions. I want you to think about better solutions than I can offer, and to talk about these problems with other furries. You’ll almost certainly go even further with your own plan than just following something that some guy wrote on a blog.

item.content:encoded:
Six years ago, I wrote a blog post titled Soatok’s Guide to Side-Channel Attacks in which I discussed the general topic of side-channels in cryptographic applications, and how to avoid them, with example code in PHP. I had called out that the algorithms discussed on the page cannot rule out compiler or runtime optimizations that undermine your security goals: You can achieve algorithmic constant-time, but any higher assurance was outside the scope of the work being done.

For that reason, we’re going to assume that algorithmic constant-time is adequate for the duration of this blog post.

If your threat model prevents you from accepting this assumption, feel free to put in the extra effort yourself and tell me how it goes. After all, as a furry who writes blog posts in my spare time for fun, I don’t exactly have the budget for massive research projects in formal verification.

Soatok’s Guide to Side-Channel Attacks (Aug. 2020)

To make it easier to see in action, I also wrote a separate TypeScript / JavaScript library called constant-time-js for demonstration purposes.

Over the years, this demo code has been adopted by precisely zero dependent packages, according to NPM (at least, as of this writing).

However, that only covers open source dependencies; I have no idea if some proprietary software decided to build on my designs.

While at a furry convention last month, I received an email from a Ph.D student named Yayu Wang which disclosed a side-channel in constant-time-js. I have since released version 0.5.0 of the library, which fixes the issue reported, and used GitHub’s security advisories feature to request a CVE.

The full credits are as follows:

Vulnerability discovered and reported by Yayu Wang. Research done by Yayu Wang, Kjell Dankert, Duy Kha Dinh, and Aastha Mehta, University of British Columbia.

My reason for posting an advisory and requesting a CVE is simple: If anyone is actually using this code (e.g., in a proprietary software system I have no visibility into), then either npm audit or a CVE being assigned is likely to trigger internal security mechanisms and prompt them to upgrade to the latest version as soon as possible.

Since the urgent stuff (advisory, patch, etc.) has already been handled elsewhere, I thought I’d write a blog post that dives deeper into the more interesting parts of this finding and its remediation.

Because, let’s be real, if you read my blog you’re either a nerd or part of a nerdy subculture, so why not nerd out a bit?

Contents

  • Timeline
  • Verifying The Report
  • Writing The Patch
  • Verifying The Fix
  • What Would Higher Assurance Look Like?

Timeline

  • 2026-08-21: Disclosure email received at 4:51 PM. I reply only to Yayu at 4:54 PM to say “Hey, I [got] your email. I’m currently traveling and will not be at a keyboard until Tuesday. I’ll follow up as soon as I can.”
  • 2026-08-25: I verify the report and then write a patch.
  • 2026-08-26: I reply-all to the disclosure email with a locally-tested proposed patch.
  • 2026-09-09: Yayu responds that they tested the patch and confirmed it removed the leakage.
  • 2026-09-10: Public disclosure and new version tagged.
  • 2026-09-11: This blog post is written.
    • Though I didn’t post it until a little after 3 AM. Oops.

Verifying The Report

In the age of AI-driven vulnerability hunting–punctuated by severity inflation and frequent hallucinations–the proportion of bogus reports to legitimate ones has increased significantly. Verifying that the bug actually exists and is as severe as the researcher claims has always been important for maintainers, but it invites much more emphasis when you’re drowning in slop.

The initial report email was shared in the pull request description for the fix, if you want to read it in full. The relevant excerpt from the description tells us enough to figure out where to start looking:

The conditional-selection functions in constant-time-js use branchless JavaScript expressions to construct selection masks. We found that select, select_alt, and select_ints nevertheless produce secret-dependent instruction- and data-cache behavior in V8. The leakage arises from V8’s ToBoolean mechanism, its different handling of -0 and -1, and direct accesses to the raw true and false Oddball objects on different cache lines. The resulting cache-access patterns can reveal the value of the selection condition.

Yayu’s disclosure email

So, obviously, the first thing to check is V8’s ToBoolean mechanism. Which looks like this:

// ToString
//
// Convert the accumulator to a String.
IGNITION_HANDLER(ToBoolean, InterpreterAssembler) {
  TNode<Object> value = GetAccumulator();
  TVARIABLE(Boolean, result);
  Label if_true(this), if_false(this), end(this);
  BranchIfToBooleanIsTrue(value, &if_true, &if_false);
  BIND(&if_true);
  {
    result = TrueConstant();
    Goto(&end);
  }
  BIND(&if_false);
  {
    result = FalseConstant();
    Goto(&end);
  }
  BIND(&end);
  SetAccumulator(result.value());
  Dispatch();
}

Oh, hey, BranchIfToBooleanIsTrue(). That name sure sounds like a branching side-channel would be exposed. And, indeed, that is what we observe.

Next, we need to look at converting from booleans. As Yayu observes:

For select, we observed that the !!returnLeft conversion reaches V8’s Builtins_ToBoolean. The true and false cases execute instructions at different addresses within the builtin.

We separately used hardware read watchpoints to measure the data addresses accessed while V8 converts the boolean condition. This confirmed direct reads from the raw true and false Oddball objects in V8’s read-only heap:

The conversion executes loads of the following form, with rdi pointing to the condition’s Oddball object:

movl   rdx, [rdi - 0x1]  // load the Oddball's map  
vmovsd xmm0, [rdi + 0x3] // load the Oddball's to_number field

Thus, the same load instruction accesses 0x...0cc for true and 0x...0b0 for false. The instruction address can be identical while its data operand reveals the condition through two different cache lines. This means that an executed-instruction trace alone can incorrectly classify the operation as constant-time; both instruction and data addresses must be considered.

This is observable from the source code, as the values for true and false are statically allocated.

  static constexpr Tagged_t kUndefinedValue = 0x69;
  static constexpr Tagged_t kNullValue = 0x85;
  static constexpr Tagged_t kempty_string = 0xa1;
  static constexpr Tagged_t kFalseValue = 0xad;
  static constexpr Tagged_t kTrueValue = 0xc9;

This lines up close to what was reported in the disclosure, except 0xc9 is one off from the 0x...0c8 from the table, and 0xad is also one off from 0x...0ac.

We can further inspect the OddBall object…

@cppObjectLayoutDefinition
@apiExposedInstanceTypeValue(0x83)
@highestInstanceTypeWithinParentClassRange
extern class Oddball extends PrimitiveHeapObject {
  to_number_raw: float64;
  to_string: String;
  to_number: Number;
  type_of: String;
  kind: Smi;
}

…and the True/False subclass definitions.

@cppObjectLayoutDefinition
@hasSameInstanceTypeAsParent
@doNotGenerateCast
extern class Boolean extends Oddball {}

@cppObjectLayoutDefinition
@hasSameInstanceTypeAsParent
@doNotGenerateCast
extern class True extends Boolean {}

@cppObjectLayoutDefinition
@hasSameInstanceTypeAsParent
@doNotGenerateCast
extern class False extends Boolean {}

This tells me that, internally, both true and false inherit from OddBall, so any of the branches that only trigger for OddBalls is relevant. This isn’t currently relevant, but is worth keeping in mind in the subsequent code snippets.

Altogether, this confirms the boolean type aspects of the report.

Observation: Avoiding booleans is the only way to be safe.

Next, we need to look at the double-negation (!!) behavior and how V8 handles signed zero, because -0 is a special value in IEEE 754 that JavaScript runtimes like V8 support, and how they support it could lead to timing leaks (as reported by Yayu).

Observe from the AccessBuilder class that HeapNumber::value_ and OddBall::to_number_raw_ are equivalent.

// static
FieldAccess AccessBuilder::ForHeapNumberOrOddballOrHoleValue() {
  STATIC_ASSERT_FIELD_OFFSETS_EQUAL(offsetof(HeapNumber, value_),
                                    offsetof(Oddball, to_number_raw_));
  STATIC_ASSERT_FIELD_OFFSETS_EQUAL(offsetof(HeapNumber, value_),
                                    Hole::kRawNumericValueOffset);
  return ForHeapNumberValue();
}

Let’s also look at unary operators, with a focus on OddBalls, to tie into the earlier analysis.

  TNode<Object> UnaryOpWithFeedback(TNode<Context> context, TNode<Object> value,
                                    TNode<UintPtrT> slot,
                                    TNode<HeapObject> maybe_feedback_vector,
                                    const SmiOperation& smi_op,
                                    const FloatOperation& float_op,
                                    const BigIntOperation& bigint_op,
                                    UpdateFeedbackMode update_feedback_mode) {
    TVARIABLE(Object, var_value, value);
    TVARIABLE(Object, var_result);
    TVARIABLE(Float64T, var_float_value);
    TVARIABLE(Smi, var_feedback, SmiConstant(BinaryOperationFeedback::kNone));
    TVARIABLE(Object, var_exception);
    Label start(this, {&var_value, &var_feedback}), end(this);
    Label do_float_op(this, &var_float_value);
    Label if_exception(this, Label::kDeferred);
    Goto(&start);
    // We might have to try again after ToNumeric conversion.
    BIND(&start);
    {
      Label if_smi(this), if_heapnumber(this), if_oddball(this);
      Label if_bigint(this, Label::kDeferred);
      Label if_other(this, Label::kDeferred);
      value = var_value.value();
      GotoIf(TaggedIsSmi(value), &if_smi);

      TNode<HeapObject> value_heap_object = CAST(value);
      TNode<Map> map = LoadMap(value_heap_object);
      GotoIf(IsHeapNumberMap(map), &if_heapnumber);
      TNode<Uint16T> instance_type = LoadMapInstanceType(map);
      GotoIf(IsBigIntInstanceType(instance_type), &if_bigint);
      Branch(InstanceTypeEqual(instance_type, ODDBALL_TYPE), &if_oddball,
             &if_other);

      BIND(&if_smi);
      {
        var_result =
            smi_op(CAST(value), &var_feedback, &do_float_op, &var_float_value);
        Goto(&end);
      }

      BIND(&if_heapnumber);
      {
        var_float_value = LoadHeapNumberValue(value_heap_object);
        Goto(&do_float_op);
      }

      BIND(&if_bigint);
      {
        var_result = bigint_op(context, value_heap_object);
        CombineFeedback(&var_feedback, BinaryOperationFeedback::kBigInt);
        Goto(&end);
      }

      BIND(&if_oddball);
      {
        // We do not require an Or with earlier feedback here because once we
        // convert the value to a number, we cannot reach this path. We can
        // only reach this path on the first pass when the feedback is kNone.
        CSA_DCHECK(this, SmiEqual(var_feedback.value(),
                                  SmiConstant(BinaryOperationFeedback::kNone)));
        OverwriteFeedback(&var_feedback,
                          BinaryOperationFeedback::kNumberOrOddball);
        var_value = LoadOddballToNumber(CAST(value_heap_object));
        Goto(&start);
      }

      BIND(&if_other);
      {
        // We do not require an Or with earlier feedback here because once we
        // convert the value to a number, we cannot reach this path. We can
        // only reach this path on the first pass when the feedback is kNone.
        CSA_DCHECK(this, SmiEqual(var_feedback.value(),
                                  SmiConstant(BinaryOperationFeedback::kNone)));
        OverwriteFeedback(&var_feedback, BinaryOperationFeedback::kAny);
        {
          ScopedExceptionHandler handler(this, &if_exception, &var_exception);
          var_value = CallBuiltin(Builtin::kNonNumberToNumeric, context,
                                  value_heap_object);
        }
        Goto(&start);
      }
    }

    BIND(&if_exception);
    {
      UpdateFeedback(var_feedback.value(), maybe_feedback_vector, slot,
                     update_feedback_mode);
      CallRuntime(Runtime::kReThrow, context, var_exception.value());
      Unreachable();
    }

    BIND(&do_float_op);
    {
      CombineFeedback(&var_feedback, BinaryOperationFeedback::kNumber);
      var_result =
          AllocateHeapNumberWithValue(float_op(var_float_value.value()));
      Goto(&end);
    }

    BIND(&end);
    UpdateFeedback(var_feedback.value(), maybe_feedback_vector, slot,
                   update_feedback_mode);
    return var_result.value();
  }

The first highlight is a branch short-circuit that runs if the feedback isn’t undefined. The second highlight explains that this feedback mechanism can only be undefined on the first pass. This is the sort of engine optimization that makes side-channel-resistant code difficult.

Finally, we must look at unary negation (affects the (-var) & 0xff pattern used in constant-time programming):

  TNode<Object> Negate(TNode<Context> context, TNode<Object> value,
                       TNode<UintPtrT> slot,
                       TNode<HeapObject> maybe_feedback_vector,
                       UpdateFeedbackMode update_feedback_mode) {
    SmiOperation smi_op =
        [=, this](TNode<Smi> smi_value, TVariable<Smi>* var_feedback,
                  Label* do_float_op, TVariable<Float64T>* var_float) {
          TVARIABLE(Number, var_result);
          Label if_zero(this), if_min_smi(this), end(this);
          // Return -0 if operand is 0.
          GotoIf(SmiEqual(smi_value, SmiConstant(0)), &if_zero);

          // Special-case the minimum Smi to avoid overflow.
          GotoIf(SmiEqual(smi_value, SmiConstant(Smi::kMinValue)), &if_min_smi);

          // Else simply subtract operand from 0.
          CombineFeedback(var_feedback, BinaryOperationFeedback::kSignedSmall);
          var_result = SmiSub(SmiConstant(0), smi_value);
          Goto(&end);

          BIND(&if_zero);
          CombineFeedback(var_feedback, BinaryOperationFeedback::kNumber);
          var_result = MinusZeroConstant();
          Goto(&end);

          BIND(&if_min_smi);
          *var_float = SmiToFloat64(smi_value);
          Goto(do_float_op);

          BIND(&end);
          return var_result.value();
        };
    FloatOperation float_op = [=, this](TNode<Float64T> float_value) {
      return Float64Neg(float_value);
    };
    BigIntOperation bigint_op = [=, this](TNode<Context> context,
                                          TNode<HeapObject> bigint_value) {
      return CAST(CallRuntime(Runtime::kBigIntUnaryOp, context, bigint_value,
                              SmiConstant(Operation::kNegate)));
    };
    return UnaryOpWithFeedback(context, value, slot, maybe_feedback_vector,
                               smi_op, float_op, bigint_op,
                               update_feedback_mode);
  }

BIND(&if_zero) returns a constant.

BIND(&if_min_smi) calls SmiToFloat64 and jumps to do_float_op. This, altogether, is not guaranteed to take the same amount of time as simply returning a constant.

Without having to compile any code or figure out how to instrument any JIT behaviors, we can be sure that this code is designed to have side-channels.

This confirms the entirety of Yayu’s report. Now that we know where the problems lie, let’s figure out how to fix them.

Writing The Patch

To arrive at the patch for the reported issues, I set the following goals for myself:

  1. Do not use the boolean type at all. That includes double-negation (!!var) or equality operators (===, !==).
  2. Do not negate-and-mask, due to how -0 (signed zero) is handled in V8.

For example, the final step of my is_nonzero function looked like this:

/**
 * Is this number anything except zero?
 *
 * @param {Uint8Array} num
 * @returns {boolean}
 */
export function is_nonzero(num: Uint8Array): boolean {
    let d: number = 0;
    for (let i: number = num.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        d |= num[i];
    }
    return d !== 0;
}

To avoid the boolean type, we can use addition and bit-shifts. However, this changes the contract for is_nonzero(), since it now returns a number. To minimize compatibility woes, we can write an internal function (called is_nonzero_flag() since it returns a bit flag as a number rather than a boolean value) and keep the existing boolean is_nonzero(), which now just calls the new function and compares its value to 1.

@@ -95,11 +95,25 @@ export function gcd(a: Uint8Array, b: Uint8Array): Uint8Array {
  * @returns {boolean}
  */
 export function is_nonzero(num: Uint8Array): boolean {
+    return is_nonzero_flag(num) === 1;
+}
+
+/**
+ * Return 1 if this number is nonzero, or 0 otherwise.
+ *
+ * This numeric form is used as input to the selection functions so that a
+ * secret-derived boolean is never passed through V8's ToBoolean machinery.
+ *
+ * @param {Uint8Array} num
+ * @returns {number}
+ */
+function is_nonzero_flag(num: Uint8Array): number {
     let d: number = 0;
     for (let i: number = num.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
         d |= num[i];
     }
-    return d !== 0;
+    // d is in [0, 255], so this maps zero to 0 and every other value to 1.
+    return (d + 0xff) >>> 8;
 }

The existing outer API still has the boolean issues, but the places is_nonzero() is used in our library was more problematic because it was called in loops over potentially secret information. See also, the implementation for pow(), whose patch looks like so:

@@ -315,7 +329,7 @@ export function pow(a: Uint8Array, n: Uint8Array): Uint8Array {
         rshift1(e, true);
         Sprime = multiply(S, S);
         S = select(
-            is_nonzero(e),
+            is_nonzero_flag(e),
             Sprime,
             normalize(S, Sprime.length)
         );

The same approach will be used to make select() constant-time.

  • Replace boolean with number, to avoid the boolean pitfalls
  • Change the mask generation strategy to not use !!
    • Since we’re no longer dealing with booleans, !!x can be (x & 1)
  • Avoid signed zeroes in interim calculations
    • -x can be replaced with 0 - (x & 1); subtracting from zero is a distinct operation from negating

The changes to select.ts are pretty short:

diff --git a/lib/select.ts b/lib/select.ts
index df6966d..7a8d4c3 100644
--- a/lib/select.ts
+++ b/lib/select.ts
@@ -1,21 +1,24 @@
 import { int32 } from './int32';
 
 /**
- * If TRUE, return left; else, return right.
+ * If choice is 1, return left; if it is 0, return right.
  *
- * @param {boolean} returnLeft
+ * @param {number} choice (0 or 1)
  * @param {Uint8Array} left
  * @param {Uint8Array} right
  * @returns {Uint8Array}
  */
-export function select(returnLeft: boolean, left: Uint8Array, right: Uint8Array): Uint8Array {
+export function select(choice: number, left: Uint8Array, right: Uint8Array): Uint8Array {
     if (left.length !== right.length) {
         throw new Error('select() expects two Uint8Array objects of equal length');
     }
     /*
-     If returnLeft, mask = 0xFF; else, mask = 0x00;
+     If choice is 1, mask = 0xFF; else, mask = 0x00.
+
+     Keep this as subtraction from positive zero. Unary negation produces -0
+     for a zero choice, which V8 represents differently from the Smi value -1.
      */
-    const mask: number = (-!!returnLeft) & 0xff;
+    const mask: number = (0 - (choice & 1)) & 0xff;
     const out: Uint8Array = new Uint8Array(left.length);
     for (let i: number = 0; i < left.length; i++) {
         out[i] = right[i] ^ ((left[i] ^ right[i]) & mask);
@@ -35,7 +38,8 @@ export function select_alt(choice: number, m: Uint8Array, n: Uint8Array): Uint8A
     if (m.length !== n.length) {
         throw new Error('Both Uint8Arrays must be the same length');
     }
-    const mask = (-choice) & 0xff;
+    // See select(): subtraction from positive zero avoids materializing -0.
+    const mask = (0 - (choice & 1)) & 0xff;
     const out = new Uint8Array(m.length);
     for (let i: number = 0; i < out.length; i++) {
         out[i] = n[i] ^ ((m[i] ^ n[i]) & mask);
@@ -55,7 +59,8 @@ export function select_ints(returnLeft: number, left: number, right: number): nu
     /*
      If returnLeft, mask = 0xFFFFFFFF; else, mask = 0x00000000;
      */
-    const mask: number = (-(returnLeft & 1)) & 0xfffffffff;
+    // See select(): subtraction from positive zero avoids materializing -0.
+    const mask: number = 0 - (returnLeft & 1);
     return right ^ ((left ^ right) & mask);
 }

At this point, I still wasn’t finished there were still some administrivia to address (tests, README updates), and I also had to fix the CI configuration. Those aren’t interesting, though. With the power of hand-waving our problems away, we move on.

Verifying The Fix

Just because the patch remediated the specific patterns that were initially reported doesn’t mean that there aren’t other leaks present. Nor does it mean that my fixes were complete.

Indeed, the is_nonzero() and pow() leakage I used as the earliest example in the previous section was identified after I fixed select() and looked for other crimes against the type system. If I had only looked at the scope of the reported issues, I might have missed that one.

But, okay. Since booleans are a lot of the problem, just avoiding using boolean variables at all is simple enough to verify: Does this code only use numbers and unary operators in places I formerly used booleans? Yes.

The other interesting question to address is: Did we successfully avoid -0?

If you recall from above, the diffs all had this pattern:

-    const mask: number = (-!!returnLeft) & 0xff;
+    const mask: number = (0 - (choice & 1)) & 0xff;

The corrected code will be interpreted as bitwise AND operations (which, if those aren’t constant-time, this whole effort is doomed) and a single subtraction from zero.

So we just need to see how subtraction is handled by V8:

TNode<Object> BinaryOpAssembler::Generate_SubtractWithFeedback(
    const LazyNode<Context>& context, TNode<Object> lhs, TNode<Object> rhs,
    TNode<UintPtrT> slot_id, const LazyNode<HeapObject>& maybe_feedback_vector,
    UpdateFeedbackMode update_feedback_mode, bool rhs_known_smi) {
  auto smiFunction = [=, this](TNode<Smi> lhs, TNode<Smi> rhs,
                               TVariable<Smi>* var_type_feedback) {
    Label end(this);
    TVARIABLE(Number, var_result);
    // If rhs is known to be an Smi (for SubSmi) we want to fast path Smi
    // operation. For the normal Sub operation, we want to fast path both
    // Smi and Number operations, so this path should not be marked as Deferred.
    Label if_overflow(this,
                      rhs_known_smi ? Label::kDeferred : Label::kNonDeferred);
    var_result = TrySmiSub(lhs, rhs, &if_overflow);
    *var_type_feedback = SmiConstant(BinaryOperationFeedback::kSignedSmall);
    Goto(&end);

    BIND(&if_overflow);
    {
      *var_type_feedback = SmiConstant(BinaryOperationFeedback::kNumber);
      TNode<Float64T> value = Float64Sub(SmiToFloat64(lhs), SmiToFloat64(rhs));
      var_result = AllocateHeapNumberWithValue(value);
      Goto(&end);
    }

    BIND(&end);
    return var_result.value();
  };
  auto floatFunction = [=, this](TNode<Float64T> lhs, TNode<Float64T> rhs) {
    return Float64Sub(lhs, rhs);
  };
  return Generate_BinaryOperationWithFeedback(
      context, lhs, rhs, slot_id, maybe_feedback_vector, smiFunction,
      floatFunction, Operation::kSubtract, update_feedback_mode, rhs_known_smi);
}

In the highlighted section, rhs_known_smi is typically false (since this is a computed value, not a bytecode immediate value). This means that the decision will be determined by TrySmiSub, with the following:

  • lhs will be 0
  • rhs will be the result of (choice & 1)

Since this doesn’t overflow (any number between INT32_MIN and INT32_MAX is not considered to have overflowed; the Smi tagging is implemented here), the if_overflow label is never jumped to.

The only things that can easily go wrong now are:

  • The compiler turns out to be evil and introduces an “optimization” that I don’t anticipate
  • The V8 developers turn out to be evil and modify how this logic works and break my assumptions in a future release
  • Other supply-chain-shaped shenanigans with package management

And, well, that’s not part of the threat model for this demo code, now is it?

When I referred to the compiler or V8 developers turning “evil” above, I meant this in a completely tongue-in-cheek way. I don’t think either party is literally malicious.

I thought this was obvious, but a Hacker News commentator took offense to that, so consider this my clarification.

Neither the V8 developer team nor the various C/C++ compiler projects give a single shit about my little demo code. Nor should they.

I’ll take “Clarifications I didn’t think needed to exist” for $300, Alex.

After I got the fix written, I generated a diff and included it in my email to Yayu, who did not observe the same leakage when they applied their methodology to the patched code.

What Would Higher Assurance Look Like?

In the previous sections, I described what efforts I took to verify the side-channel vulnerability was real, how I wrote the patch, and how I checked that the patch actually solves the problem.

Some people will read this and wonder, “Why are we even trying to do this in JavaScript?”

The only way we solve the “don’t roll your own crypto” problem is if we meet developers halfway. Give them high-quality tools that solve their problem that undergo expert scrutiny, and they will have no reason to roll their own crypto.

Many developers who find themselves needing cryptography tools are writing software in languages that security geeks and cryptographers do not willingly or readily use for their work.

To that end, I take it upon myself to at least make an effort to satisfy their unmet needs.

But a more interesting question to consider is, “Can we do even better?”

One tempting solution is to write all of our cryptography in Rust (or some other security nerd approved language), compile the algorithms into WebAssembly (or, if you’re only server-side, FFI it instead), and not try to make interpreted code isochronic.

Unfortunately, there is no real constant-time guarantee for WebAssembly. As of this writing, a proposal exists, but it hasn’t been updated in 4 years.

While we’re talking about it, there really isn’t (broadly speaking) any guarantee around systems programming languages (C, Rust, etc.), either.

However, there is ongoing work to make that happen.

Closing Thoughts

I hope this was an interesting enough dive into the side-channel vulnerability I accidentally introduced in my demo code.

The header art was made by AJ_LovesDinos.

item.content:encoded:
Last month, I attended both DEFCON and Megaplex. If you’re not familiar with either event, here’s all you need to know.

DEFCON is a hacker convention with a substantial furry presence.

Megaplex is a furry convention with a substantial hacker presence.

If you’ve never attended either event, here’s a few essential things to remember:

  1. You choose your own adventure. Everything is multi-track. You cannot possibly attend every event on the schedule. Choose a few must-see events, and don’t be mad at yourself if you still end up missing one.
  2. The convention is irreducible to the schedule. For some people, the most memorable events won’t be found in a meetup or panel. The “hallway track” (informal meetups and encounters between friends or even kind strangers) can be incredibly rewarding.
  3. Almost everyone is a volunteer. You aren’t at a theme park, you’re surrounded by people with shared interests.
  4. Remember to respect consent and boundaries. For example: Don’t take photos of a fursuiter having a wardrobe malfunction. Wait until they’ve fixed it and they might even pose with you!
    1. Also, most fursuits have very poor vision, so if you think a fursuiter is ignoring you, they probably didn’t see you.

I like to spend my conventions hanging out with friends and meeting cool people. I usually dedicate several hours to simply being in fursuit and wandering around.

Sometimes, folks recognize me as the author of this blog. Rarely, someone will look at me and yell the wrong species (“Kitty!”).

Interestingly enough, despite doing two cons back-to-back, I don’t actually have many photos of myself in my fursuit.

This shouldn’t be too surprising, if you remember that I write long-form technical content rather than attention-grabbing reels on TikTok or YouTube Shorts.

Hell, I can barely dance, and that was only due to the efforts of a kind tiger and his other friends.

With the furry fandom continuing to grow at a breakneck exponential rate, this means that the probability of any given furry knowing about me (or even caring to know) approaches zero at a rate proportional to the fandom’s growth. Personal irrelevance is inevitable for this blog.

Of course, that doesn’t mean that I spent all my time like this:

Influencers and Other Blights

Every once in a while, some random media influencer with a 6+ digit follower count decides to make a video about “what really goes on” at furry conventions. I won’t link any examples, but it’s a recurring topic.

But then you find gems like this:

If you haven’t watched Bekah’s video yet, and might want to, stop reading until you do. What I say after the next photo will spoil one of the more emotionally impactful parts of her video.

In their desperate search for scandalous footage, self-proclaimed influencers whose only purpose in life is to provide clickbait filler between advertisements sure do miss a lot about their actual thesis.

I was mildly astonished that Bekah actually showed the memorial wall for the members of our community that have died. She shows more authenticity in her work than I’ve come to expect from YouTubers.

I don’t think I could ever trust any of the Discount Logan Pauls running around on multimedia platforms spreading mockery and ridicule to actually give a shit about the furry fandom or its members. But if they did actually care–if they had a modicum of respect or empathy for the people they’re trying to make a spectacle out of–they would find so much more interesting drama beneath the surface.

Not all furry discourse is the usual suspects.

Two Certainties: Death and Foxes

I’m writing this with the trust that nobody that reads my blog will try to start problems or harass anyone.

However, to make this expectation a bit more difficult to violate, I’m not including any names.

A few years ago, a friend of mine died. I found out when his boyfriend posted about it on Twitter and made it all about himself rather than my friend. Later, I found out that his boyfriend held a “seance” over VRChat in order to decide whether to attend a furry convention days later.

And, look, we all grieve differently, but to say that finding out that way didn’t hurt and piss me off would be a fucking lie.

This whole fucking ordeal could have unfolded right in front of one of these YouTube chucklefucks and they would be oblivious. They’d either cut the footage entirely because it doesn’t serve the “furries are sex-crazed losers” narrative they were gunning for, or make up some bullshit about it all secretly being a cult. And then jump-cut to them disrupting the dance competition or some shit.

My friend’s death was, at least in part, the result of his younger years of excessive alcohol use. In many of our private conversations, he talked about the pain of losing his ex to said ex’s drunk driving. But most of our conversations were forward-looking.

After his late grandmother had died and he received an inheritance, he invested some of it into a career change and planned to use the rest of it to help other furries with their own careers and financial security. I had written Furward Momentum the year before, so we ended up talking about that sort of thing a lot.

Trying to pretend that the lives of millions of people can fit into the same mold and/or soundbite is the kind of hubris that only dysfunctional institutions can believe is normal.

A few years ago, Joaquin Baldwin shared this sketch while recalling a conversation with Roe Grayfox:

If your narrative about a community cannot encapsulate moments like this, you’re probably lying whether you realize it or not.

Much Abuzz About “Fleas”

While I was fursuiting at Megaplex, someone clipped a clothespin to my tail without my notice until I got back to my hotel room, hours later. It had the word “flea” written on it in permanent marker.

Reasonable people can have different opinions about this.

Unreasonable people will insist that, if you don’t want strangers secretly attaching foreign objects to your thousand-dollar wearable work of art as part of an activity that isn’t officially on the convention’s programming, then “don’t go to cons” (archive).

Unreasonable people will harass and generally be nasty to the person that created the “fleas”.

Ad-supported social media platforms are incentivized to amplify the unreasonable.

If you talk to a person with even a modicum of sense, you’ll get a spectrum of answers, which can be bucketed roughly like:

  • Oh, yeah, it’s cute and funny and whimsical. “I got fleas at the furry con!” Haha, good show, furries! Keep it up!
  • I get the humor, but I’m not personally comfortable with people touching me without my knowledge and consent.
  • What if folks started clipping airtags to fursuiters without their permission? This could easily normalize stalker behavior.
  • Meh, at least nobody’s being sexually harassed or assaulted.

One friend described it like taping a “kick me” sign to someone: If you’re doing it to a friend, then good fun and humor are almost certainly involved. If you’re doing it to a stranger, and then someone else actually kicks them because of it? Yikes.

Like, the goddamn sky isn’t falling either way, but we should probably as a community decide how we want to handle this conduct. None of that conversation requires anyone be nasty to anyone else. Put down the fucking beware doc.

The Renaissance Of Furry Aversion

Recently, the Maryland Renaissance Festival decided to ban fursuits. If you’re suppressing a yawn at that headline, take a look at how this was announced on social media (archive):

It’s a private event with a dress code. Not every venue has to accommodate every subculture — and “discrimination” doesn’t automatically mean someone’s rights were violated.

Hmm. What did they mean by this?

Renaissance festivals are a lot of fun, but (at least in Florida, where I live) they’re not really equipped for fursuiting. They don’t have anything like an air conditioned Headless Lounge nor adequate water available.

Trying to fursuit at an outdoor event without the infrastructure needed to make it safe for attendees is certainly a choice that only the most dedicated of nerds would consider.

But singling out furries instead of other period-inaccurate garb (e.g., Star Wars) is at least a little suspicious, since only the furry community is really noteworthy for being overwhelmingly LGBTQIA+.

But who knows? Maybe there’s a furry in Maryland that personally ruined it for everyone. Stranger things have happened.

You Can’t Spell FAIL Without AI

Speaking of renaissances, we need to talk about AI.

While I was at DEFCON, I estimate about 10% of the people that I talked to were either currently unemployed or extremely anxious about their income being displaced by management’s investments in AI.

Generative AI has never been popular among furries. Anything that harms artists isn’t going to be popular in a community of artists and their patrons. Add in the misinformation angle, juxtaposed with the baseless litterbox hoax, and you’ve got a recipe for conflict.

In the past, I’ve neglected to cover AI on this blog (aside from complaining about the lack of consent in companies’ decisionmaking), for a few distinct reasons:

  1. I don’t want to accidentally help the jerks who want to harm my community, nor the people who directly benefit from hyping up and subsequently bursting a bubble.
  2. Too many other people are talking about it, and I’m burned out on hearing about it all the damn time.

However, some of the anti-AI folks have taken their cause into a weird direction by engaging in what one friend described as “outright reality denial”. This observation has precipitated beyond just discussions about LLMs.

In reality (whether or not anyone finds it convenient), AI can do useful work. There isn’t really much space for opinions or beliefs; it’s a measurable, empirical observation about the world we live in today.

As I write this, OpenAI is claiming a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem. This has led to statements from other mathematicians. Terrence Tao weighed in too. Even if this turns out to be a correct solution, it doesn’t change the fact that it’s also a marketing stunt.

The main competitor to OpenAI is a company called Anthropic, whose CEO writes MST3K-worthy essays with titles like Machines of Loving Grace that feel like “What if Jim Jones read LessWrong?” and whose wife (and key strategic advisor) contacted Jeffrey Epstein years after his conviction to pitch a “luxury porn” startup.

All of the other players in this space are legacy BigTech corporations whose brutal policy decisions have a body count that would make some PMCs envious if they weren’t directed at their own employees and/or customers.

Possibly the cruelest part about this whole shitshow is how much AI enthusiasm is driven by fooling oneself.

Here’s a fun exercise: Clone a random security startup’s “skill” repo off GitHub and measure how many lines of it are Markdown instructions or TOML config defining different characters for the machine to roleplay, and compare it with lines of actual code. How much of that Markdown is reminding Claude what a SQL injection vulnerability looks like, as if it wasn’t absorbed into its training data?

Then, is it any wonder that the Internet is nigh-unusable due to the prevalence of AI bots that scrape webpages over and over instead of just cloning a repo locally?

Ever since my employer mandated the use of AI last year, the key difference I’ve observed between successful projects (whether development or security scanning) is the commitment to engineering best practices.

Y’know, the boring shit? Eating your wheaties?

To put it a bit more blunt, if you’re required to use AI at work and want to get anything useful, you need at least two things:

  1. A good definition of “done”
  2. A tight feedback loop

AI enthusiasts could probably point an LLM at my Public Key Directory specification and get a working client in virtually any programming language due to the assurance practices I’ve been strictly adhering to. Of course, their coding agent will get all the credit if they do.

There are so many more interesting ways to be critical of this hellscape than trying to pretend that the technology is little more sophisticated than your iPhone’s “next word prediction” feature.

The biggest problem with AI is people.

Nobody reasonable is mad at linear algebra or computer science. Gradient descent, neural networks, transformer models, reinforcement learning, etc. are socially neutral concepts, inherently.

The wealthy investor class that hopes AI will displace entire industries’ workforces suck.

The CEOs and middle managers that decimate their workforce while enjoying record-breaking profits suck.

The people who use AI to spread misinformation and propaganda on social media suck.

The botlickers (sic) eager to sacrifice their neighbors and the environment for more cloud compute suck.

The grifters who use AI “art” to create profiles to try to blend in to subcultures they have no real interest in suck.

But as much as I do begrudge the people who changed the material conditions of our industry over the past few years in pursuit of their self-interest for the various harms they’ve caused, I do not extend this contempt towards junior developers or anyone at risk of losing their income tomorrow.

Just as you have to put on your own oxygen mask before you help others, do what you have to in order to survive the changing climate.

If reasonably practical, I do encourage you to find some way to maintain your independence: a way to do the basic skills that are now being automated without relying on any cloud-based service. Otherwise, those skills will almost certainly atrophy over time. There’s no such thing as a free lunch, after all.

Closing Remarks

This has been another grab-bag blog post stitched out of smaller topics that didn’t quite make the cut for a dedicated, focused writing.

I do these from time to time. A few people have complained about topic whiplash, so I’ve tried to make the transitions a bit less jarring this time around.

I’m planning to contribute to the DEFCON Furs badge puzzle for 2027. I’ve also offered to contribute cryptographic puzzles to Megaplex since their theme next year is Curse of Anubis, which has a lot of potential.

One of these days, I’m going to submit a CRYPTO rump session for a Fresh Prince of Bel-Air parody song titled Fresh Prints of Bellare. This will either force me to attend CRYPTO in fursuit, or mildly annoy the cryptography community.

Header photo was taken by yosh at Megaplex 2026.
